opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one of the most important qualities right now is speed. With generative AI, the cost of building prototypes has collapsed. Something that used to take a team six months, a small team can now build in a weekend. So the founders I see succeeding are the ones who move really fast: they build, put it in front of users, get feedback, and iterate rapidly. Speed is a strong predictor of success in startups, and AI has made it even more important.

The second thing is being concrete. At AI Fund, we've found that vague ideas like "let's use AI to improve healthcare" are hard to act on. A concrete idea, something specific enough that an engineer can go and build it, lets you move fast and quickly find out whether it's right or wrong. If it's wrong, that's fine. You pivot. Concreteness is what makes speed possible.

Third, I think technical depth matters a lot. The technology is changing so quickly, with new models, agentic workflows, and better tooling every few months, that founders who really understand it have a big edge. They have better intuitions about what's now feasible that wasn't feasible six months ago, and many of the best opportunities sit right at that frontier.

Finally, as building gets cheaper, the bottleneck is shifting to product management: deciding what to build. So founders who combine technical understanding with deep empathy for users, people who can talk to customers and quickly make good product decisions, are in a really strong position. When engineering gets ten times faster, figuring out what users actually want becomes the scarce skill.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes speed, concrete ideas, technical depth, and product judgment, but does not recommend reassessing workflows created before recent generative AI advances.

r002.rationale: It says founders with technical depth have an edge, but does not compare them with business-savvy founders who lack a feel for AI’s direction.

r003.rationale: The response connects technical understanding to recognizing what is feasible and making product decisions, but does not state that forming company strategy is difficult without understanding AI’s capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest one, honestly, is speed. The cost of building a prototype has fallen so dramatically that the bottleneck is no longer "can we build it," it's "can we figure out what to build." So the founders I see doing well are the ones who can run many fast, cheap experiments, look at the results, and update their beliefs quickly. If you can go from an idea to a working prototype in a day instead of a quarter, you get to learn ten or twenty times as much as your competitors, and that compounds.

Related to that, I've become a big believer in concrete ideas. A lot of founders come to me with something like "we'll use AI to transform healthcare." That's not an idea you can build on Monday. "We'll let a radiologist dictate notes and have an agent pre-fill the insurance form" is. You might be wrong, but you'll find out fast. Vague ideas feel safe because nobody can say they're wrong, and that's exactly why they're dangerous.

The second thing is technical depth, and I'll say something a little contrarian here. People sometimes assume that as AI gets more capable, understanding the technology matters less, because the tools do it for you. I've found the opposite. The founders who actually understand how an LLM behaves, what agentic workflows can and can't do, when to fine-tune versus prompt, when to use RAG, those founders see opportunities that others just can't see. The technology is moving so quickly that there's a lot of what I'd call "alpha" in simply knowing what's now possible that wasn't possible six months ago. A lot of great businesses right now are basically people noticing that something that was impossible last year is suddenly easy.

And third, I'd say a willingness to go find a real customer and a real problem, often in some unglamorous domain. The foundation model layer gets all the attention, but the application layer is where most of the value is going to be created, and that means talking to people in logistics, or legal, or manufacturing, and understanding their workflow well enough to build something they'll actually pay for.

So if I had to compress it: move fast, be concrete, understand the technology deeply, and stay close to real problems. None of that is new advice, exactly, but generative AI has turned the dial on all of it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends fast experimentation and concrete ideas, but does not discuss reassessing workflows retained from before recent generative AI advances.

r002.rationale: It says founders who understand AI technology can spot opportunities, but does not compare their likelihood of success with business-savvy founders who lack a feel for where AI is heading.

r003.rationale: The response says technical understanding helps founders see opportunities, but does not state that forming company strategy is difficult without understanding AI capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most important qualities is the ability to learn quickly. Generative AI is changing rapidly, so a founder needs to be willing to update their assumptions—about what the technology can do, what customers want, and what’s actually difficult to build.

I’d also look for a combination of technical understanding and deep curiosity about a customer’s problem. It’s relatively easy to build an impressive demo. It’s much harder to understand someone’s workflow well enough to build something they’ll use every day and pay for.

And then there’s speed of execution. Can you talk to customers, build something, test it, and learn from the result? A founder who runs that cycle quickly has more opportunities to discover something valuable. You don’t need to predict every advance in AI. You need to recognize when an advance creates an opportunity, and be able to act on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses updating assumptions and understanding customer workflows, but does not recommend reassessing workflows retained from before recent generative AI advances.

r002.rationale: It values technical understanding and noticing AI opportunities, but does not compare founders who stay current with AI to business-savvy founders who lack a feel for AI’s direction.

r003.rationale: It says founders should update assumptions about what the technology can do, but does not state that forming company strategy is difficult without that understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most important qualities is the ability to learn quickly. With generative AI, the technology changes so rapidly that a founder’s current knowledge matters less than their ability to keep updating it—and to turn what they learn into something useful for customers.

I also look for people who are very hands-on. It’s become much cheaper to build a prototype, put it in front of users, and see what happens. So a small team that can run that cycle quickly has a lot of opportunity. But you still need the judgment to ask: Are we solving a real problem? Does someone care enough about this to use it or pay for it?

And then there’s persistence, coupled with flexibility. You want to be committed to helping a particular set of customers, while being willing to change your assumptions about the product. If an underlying model improves and makes your original approach obsolete, can you use that improvement to deliver something even better? I think that’s a very valuable mindset for a founder right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses updating knowledge and adapting a product, but does not recommend reassessing workflows retained from before recent generative AI advances.

r002.rationale: It values learning quickly as technology changes, but does not compare technologically current founders with business-savvy founders who lack a feel for AI’s direction.

r003.rationale: It does not state that forming company strategy is difficult without understanding AI’s capabilities.
